hints: Count the carbons carefully, chloroethane has two carbons but propanoate has three, so Q must add one extra carbon.
Remember that boiling aqueous NaOH hydrolyses a nitrile to a carboxylate salt, so Q must be propanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$.
Think about how to swap $\text{Cl}$ for $\text{CN}$ by nucleophilic substitution, and which source of cyanide works for a halogenoalkane.
walkthrough:
**Count carbons to spot chain lengthening**

Chloroethane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ with 2 carbons. Sodium propanoate is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ with 3 carbons. So the first step must add one carbon.

$$\text{C}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_3$$

**Identify Q from its hydrolysis**

Nitriles hydrolyse with boiling aqueous NaOH to give carboxylate salts plus ammonia. That tells us Q is a nitrile.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{NH}_3$$

**Choose the reagent for halogenoalkane to nitrile**

Chloroethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution where $\text{CN}^-$ replaces $\text{Cl}$. This needs ionic cyanide in ethanolic solution to act as a nucleophile.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Cl}^-$$

**Pick the correct cyanide conditions**

Potassium cyanide in ethanol provides free $\text{CN}^-$ for substitution on a halogenoalkane. This gives Q as propanenitrile, ready for hydrolysis.

options.A: Concentrated ammonia gives nucleophilic substitution to an amine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Amines do not hydrolyse with NaOH to give carboxylates, and no carbon is added.
options.B: Dilute sulfuric acid does not convert a chloroalkane to a nitrile. It adds no carbon and cannot provide $\text{CN}^-$, so Q could not form.
options.C: Hydrogen cyanide in water is the reagent for nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones to make hydroxynitriles, not for substitution on halogenoalkanes. It is largely molecular $\text{HCN}$ and a poor source of $\text{CN}^-$ for this reaction.
options.D: Potassium cyanide in ethanol provides $\text{CN}^-$ which substitutes $\text{Cl}$ in chloroethane to give propanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. This is Q, which then hydrolyses with boiling aqueous NaOH to sodium propanoate. Ethanolic conditions favour substitution over hydrolysis.
